how-much-to-charge-for-a-retaining-wall..text:
← Retaining wall bid calculator

How much to charge for a retaining wall

Price the job from cost, then convert to dollars per linear foot. Do not start from a published per-foot number and work backwards. Two 40-foot walls can differ by several thousand dollars once height, drainage, geogrid, and an engineer stamp are in the bid.

Open the free bid calculator

What a per-foot quote cannot see

Homeowners shop length. These do not scale with length alone:

  • Face area — length × (exposed height + embedment). Twice the height is twice the block, plus more stone behind it
  • Drain-stone volume and a perforated pipe that has to run the whole wall
  • Geogrid layers that typically appear around 4 ft exposed and add a layer every couple of feet after that
  • A 90° corner — extra cuts that stay the same on a 30 ft wall as on an 80 ft wall
  • An engineer stamp and a permit, which many jurisdictions treat as a step near 4 ft, not a foot
  • Machine time, dump fees, and travel that are a trip, not a linear foot

If you match a cheaper per-foot quote that was written for a 3 ft garden wall, you are matching someone else's job, not yours.

A bid that holds together

  1. Measure length, exposed height, and embedment. Face area is the takeoff, not length.
  2. Price block and cap from face area and length. Price drain stone from cubic yards, not a guess.
  3. Add geogrid as its own layers × depth × cost. Zero layers on a short garden wall is a decision, not a default forever.
  4. Time face labor as hours per square foot on easy access, then multiply by wall type and height.
  5. Add corners, excavation, and drain placement as their own hours. They do not shrink when the wall is short and tall.
  6. Load the wage (taxes, workers' compensation, insurance, PTO). Price from loaded labor, not take-home.
  7. Add engineer, permit, travel, and machine as their own line.
  8. Recover overhead as a percent of direct cost, then set margin as a share of the customer's price.
  9. Only then look at price per foot — and at the walk-away price if a homeowner asks you to sharpen it.

What this is not

This is not an engineered wall design, a soils report, a manufacturer table, a permit approval, a code inspection, or tax advice. It is arithmetic on numbers you enter. Confirm soils, drainage, geogrid, embedment, and every invoice before you send a price.

It is also not a fence bid, a concrete slab bid, or a deck bid. Those are different jobs. This prices a stacked or formed retaining face plus the drainage and reinforcement that face actually requires.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a retaining wall?

Charge from your own cost: face area (length times total height including embedment), block and cap, drain-stone volume, perforated pipe, geogrid layers, crew hours times a wall-type and height factor, corners, excavation, engineer and permit fees, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. Convert that price to dollars per linear foot at the end for comparison, not as the bid method.

Why is a per-linear-foot quote dangerous?

Length is the number homeowners shop. Height cubes material and labor. Drain stone, geogrid, and often an engineer stamp appear as height grows. A 40 ft, 6 ft engineered wall is not twice a 40 ft, 3 ft garden wall — it is a different job. Matching a cheaper per-foot quote written for the short wall is how a sold job becomes a loss.

Does this include an engineered design or a permit?

No. The calculator prices the install from numbers you enter. Soils, manufacturer tables, geogrid design, permits, and inspections are the contractor's, the engineer's, or the AHJ's to apply. Do not treat the tool as a design, code, or soils determination.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or soils advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR HARDSCAPE AND LANDSCAPE CONTRACTORS

Bid the height and the drain, not the linear foot.

A flat per-foot quote treats a 40 ft, 3 ft garden wall as the same job as a 40 ft, 6 ft engineered wall. Face area, drain-stone volume, and geogrid layers grow with height. An engineer stamp does not shrink on a short, tall wall. Price those extras separately — then see the price, the dollars per foot, and the number below which the job loses money.

The wall

Start from a common residential wall, then replace length and height with the job you actually walked.

Height, drainage, and extras

Height multiplies face labor. Drain stone grows with face area. Geogrid layers and engineer fees are a step, not a foot. Corners are extra cuts that do not get cheaper on a short wall.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. Matching a cheaper per-foot quote after leaving it out is how a sold job becomes a loss.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the homeowner — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the cost goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Wall-type factors, height factors, and extras are common ballpark starting points, not an industry standard, a benchmark, an engineered design, or a guarantee. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why does a per-linear-foot price for a retaining wall go wrong?

    Because almost nothing in a wall is priced by the foot. Face material is bought by the square foot of face, which is length × (exposed height + embedment). Drain stone is a volume behind the wall. Geogrid is square yards per layer, and taller walls need more layers. An engineer stamp and a permit arrive as a step, not a foot. A 40 ft wall at 3 ft and a 40 ft wall at 6 ft are the same linear feet and roughly double the face, more than double the stone, and two geogrid layers apart.

    Why is buried height counted when the customer only sees the exposed part?

    Because you still build it. Embedment — the course or so below grade that keeps the wall from kicking out — is block you buy, set, and backfill, and it is invisible in the height the homeowner quotes back at you. Face area here is length × (exposed + embedment) for exactly that reason. The cap, by contrast, really is per foot of length, so it is priced that way.

    How many geogrid layers does a wall need?

    The starting count here is: none under 4 ft exposed, one layer at 4 ft, and one more for every additional 2 ft. So a 6 ft wall starts at two layers and an 8 ft wall at three. That is a starting count for pricing, not a design — actual reinforcement depends on the soil, the surcharge, the block, and the manufacturer's tables, and above about 4 ft that is an engineer's determination, not a calculator's. Each layer costs square yards of grid across the wall length at the depth it runs back, plus the labor to place it.

    When does an engineer or a permit enter the price?

    Many US jurisdictions treat roughly 4 ft of exposed height as the line, which is why the options here are none, permit only (starting around $250), and engineer stamp plus permit (starting around $1,800). Those are starting figures to replace with your own, and the threshold is a common pattern rather than a rule — confirm it with your building department for the specific site before you quote. Getting this wrong is the single most expensive omission in a wall bid, because it is thousands of dollars that no per-foot number contains.

    How does the wall type change the labor?

    It multiplies face hours: segmental block is the 1.0 baseline, timber or sleeper 0.9, boulder or natural stone 1.3, and poured formed concrete 1.4. Height multiplies face hours again — 1.0 for a garden wall under 3 ft, 1.1 for 3–4 ft, 1.25 for 4–6 ft, and 1.45 above that — because taller walls mean more lifts, more compaction, and often a machine at the face. Excavation, drainage, and corners stay separate: the excavator shows up once whatever the wall's height, and the drain pipe still runs the length.

    Why isn't a 25% margin the same as adding 25% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the customer and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $9,000 cost marked up 25% is $11,250, a 20% margin; a 25% target margin is $12,000. vs-a-flat-140-per-linear-foot-rate.html.text:
← Retaining Wall Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $140-a-linear-foot rate

"$140 a linear foot" is not a price for a retaining wall — it is a price for a 40 ft, 3 ft garden wall, quietly applied to every taller, geogrid-reinforced, cornered, or engineered wall the truck pulls up to.

What a flat $140-a-linear-foot rate is

A flat rate per linear foot is the number every homeowner can check with a tape measure along the ground, which is exactly why it is also the number competing bids get compared on. It is fast to quote over the phone and easy to put on a postcard: one number, times the run's length, read back as a total.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the shortest, lowest wall a company is willing to quote sight unseen: a 40 ft run at 3 ft exposed, segmental block, no corners, no geogrid, no engineer stamp, no permit — and then reused for every wall afterward, whether or not the next one looks anything like that wall.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the wall's length, exposed height, embedment below grade, wall type, drain-stone volume, geogrid layers, corners, and the engineer/permit step, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the face area, the drainage, the geogrid, and the extras separately, and returns a walk-away price for the wall you describe — for this wall, not a generic one.

Wall$140/lf rateBreak-even costWalk-away priceActual margin
The rate's own job: 40×3 garden wall, segmental block$5,600.00$4,269.06$5,473.1623.8%, close to the 22% target
40 ft × 4 ft, first geogrid layer$5,600.00$5,840.12$7,487.33−4.3%, a $240.12 loss
50 ft × 6 ft engineered, two geogrid layers$7,000.00$10,093.35$12,940.20−44.2%, a $3,093.35 loss
80 ft × 4 ft with two corners$11,200.00$10,996.45$14,098.011.8%, $203.55 over cost

Worked using this calculator's own shipped wall presets at a $38 crew wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 22% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator's wall presets to check any row yourself.

What a flat rate per linear foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a 3 ft garden wall and a 6 ft engineered wall, even though face area — length times exposed-plus-embedment height — roughly doubles between them. Prices face material and face labor from length times total height, so a taller wall costs more per foot, not the same per foot.
Has no separate line for drain stone or geogrid, so a wall needing two reinforcement layers is quoted the same as one needing none. Prices drain-stone volume and geogrid square yards from the entered depth and layer count, so reinforcement shows up as real material and labor.
Ignores the engineer stamp and permit fee that many jurisdictions require once a wall clears roughly 4 ft exposed — often the single largest line a per-foot rate misses. Adds the entered engineer-and-permit fee as its own cost, so a tall wall's paperwork shows up in the price before the crew is on site.
Bakes payroll burden into a round per-foot number nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a rate to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper flat rate on a harder wall. Reports a walk-away price built from the entered scope, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost and target margin before the crew commits to it.

A flat rate per linear foot is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one wall it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market or an engineer's determination on a tall wall; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $140-a-linear-foot retaining-wall rate get the price wrong?

Because linear feet is only the measurement a homeowner can read off a tape measure along the ground. Almost nothing else in a wall scales with it. Face material is bought by the square foot of face -- length times (exposed height plus embedment) -- so a taller wall means more face for the same length. Drain stone is a volume behind the wall. Geogrid is square yards per layer, and taller walls need more layers: none under 4 ft exposed, one at 4 ft, another every 2 ft after that. An engineer stamp and a permit arrive as a step, not a foot, once a wall clears the height most jurisdictions treat as the line. A flat per-foot rate charges all of that the same as the shortest wall it was set on.

What job is the $140-a-linear-foot number actually built around?

One specific job, usually the shortest, shortest-height wall a company is willing to quote off a phone call: a 40 ft run at 3 ft exposed, segmental block, no corners, no geogrid, no engineer or permit. It is a marketing price meant to win the estimate over a competitor's bid, not a number derived from any particular wall's height, drainage, or geogrid.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped wall presets, at a $38 crew wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 22% target margin: the 40 ft, 3 ft garden wall the $140 rate is named for costs $4,269.06 to build and this calculator prices it at $5,473.16, so the flat $5,600.00 rate actually clears a 23.8% margin on it -- close to the shop's own 22% target. But the same $140/lf on a 40 ft, 4 ft wall needing its first geogrid layer reproduces $5,600.00 against a $5,840.12 break-even cost -- a -4.3% margin, a $240.12 loss, not a profit. On a 50 ft, 6 ft engineered wall with two geogrid layers, the flat $7,000.00 loses $3,093.35 against this calculator's $10,093.35 cost, a -44.2% margin. And an 80 ft wall at 4 ft with two corners nets a thin 1.8% margin -- $203.55 over cost -- on a flat $11,200.00, against this calculator's $14,098.01 walk-away price.

Is a flat rate per linear foot ever the right way to quote a retaining wall?

For a short wall close to the one the rate was priced on, a flat rate can land close to a fair margin -- this calculator's own numbers show $140/lf clearing near the target margin on the easiest preset. The risk is quoting a taller, geogrid-reinforced, cornered, or engineered wall at the same rate sight unseen, because the rate does not know the face area, the drain-stone volume, the geogrid layers, or the engineer step until the takeoff is actually done, and that is exactly where the job stops being profitable.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates, and it is not an engineered wall design, a permit approval, or a geotechnical determination. It takes the length, exposed height, embedment, wall type, drainage, geogrid layers, corners, and the engineer/permit step you enter, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this wall -- the arithmetic a flat per-linear-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-linear-foot rate is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the wall stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

vs-aspire.html.text:
← Retaining Wall Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a hardscape or landscape company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this retaining wall cost, given its height, drainage, and geogrid — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton, headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri. It is built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors — including hardscape and retaining-wall crews — as well as irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning companies, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with a mobile app for crews in the field. Its own plans are tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold at one flat price, and no dollar figure for any plan is published on its site — pricing is reached by requesting a demo. Aspire's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact tier names or any dollar figure, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a business-management platform serving landscape construction, irrigation, snow and ice, and cleaning contractors, sold as a revenue-tiered subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Aspire appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one wall — length, exposed height, and embedment below grade, wall type (segmental block, timber, poured concrete, or boulder), drain-stone volume, geogrid layers, 90° corners, and whether the job needs a permit only or an engineer stamp plus permit — plus loaded crew cost, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the install price, the price per linear foot, the price per face square foot, the effective crew hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one wall. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

I run a hardscape or landscape company and need leads, estimates, scheduling, purchasing, and invoicing tracked in one system across every crew and every job.Aspire, or a comparable business-management platform — running the whole operation is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this retaining wall, given its height, embedment, drainage, and geogrid?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much does going from a 3 ft garden wall to a 6 ft engineered wall actually add, beyond the extra linear feet?This calculator's separate face-area, drain-stone, and geogrid-layer line items — a flat per-foot rate hides all three.
A customer's budget is below what I'd normally quote. Does it still clear my walk-away floor?This calculator's proposed-price check — it flags a price below break-even before you agree to it.
I need my whole crew scheduling, purchasing, and job costing running from one shared account across the season.Aspire — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a retaining-wall bid actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Aspire is used through a subscription account, and its site describes plans as scaled to a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold to a solo operator at a flat price.

Most hardscape and landscape companies get different value from each: Aspire (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole lead-to-invoice operation as an ongoing, revenue-tiered subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one retaining wall should cost from its height, drainage, and geogrid before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a scheduled job, or a signed contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or Aspire?

They do different jobs, and a hardscape or landscape company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Aspire, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton and headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri, is a cloud business-management platform built for landscape maintenance and construction (including hardscape and retaining-wall crews), irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning contractors, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it.
